heuristic: Recruit your first users manually and give them unscalably good treatment; scalable channels come after the product works.
Launch fast, because getting version 1 in front of users is the only way to learn what you should have been building.
A startup is a company designed to grow fast, and growth rate is the compass for nearly every decision it makes.
Know whether you are default alive or default dead on current trajectory before entertaining any expansive plan.
Treat fundraising as a discrete phase: be in fundraising mode or out of it, close quickly, and get back to building.

Avoid raising too much: an oversized round at a high valuation sets a bar the next raise must clear, and the extra money gets spent, mostly on people, which makes the company rigid; if you do raise a huge amount, do not spend it.
A startup compresses a working life into a few years of deliberate, maximum intensity.
Build a lean MVP in weeks, holding the problem tightly and the solution loosely, and iterate with real users.

source.author: Michael Seibel
source.work: How to Plan an MVP (YC Startup School talk)

heuristic: Focus is a force multiplier: work out what matters most, say no to almost everything else, and move fast on what remains.
Treat every product and strategy decision as a hypothesis, and run the smallest build-measure-learn loop that can validate or kill it.
The facts you need live outside the building, so test every business-model hypothesis directly with customers before scaling anything.
No business plan survives first contact with customers, so run a search for a working business model instead of executing a plan.

source.author: Steve Blank
source.work: No Plan Survives First Contact With Customers – Business Plans versus Business Models

heuristic: When validating an idea, ask about the customer's life and past behavior; never pitch and never ask whether they would buy.
Launch early enough that the first version embarrasses you; if it does not, you launched too late.

source.author: Reid Hoffman
source.work: If There Aren't Any Typos In This Essay, We Launched Too Late!

heuristic: When a winner-take-most market is up for grabs, prioritize speed over efficiency, accepting risk and waste to reach scale first.
While blitzscaling, triage ruthlessly: decide which fires you will let burn rather than trying to fix every problem.
Build half a product, not a half-assed product: cut scope aggressively and keep the quality of what ships high.

source.author: Jason Fried, David Heinemeier Hansson, and Matt Linderman

heuristic: Run a calm company: sustainable 40-hour weeks and a long-term pace beat chaos, crunch, and manufactured urgency.

source.author: Jason Fried and David Heinemeier Hansson
source.work: It Doesn't Have to Be Crazy at Work

heuristic: Reject the unicorn-or-bust frame: a profitable, independent company serving its customers is a complete success without venture capital.
Climb the stair step: start with small one-time products, build to recurring revenue, and only then attempt the ambitious standalone company.

source.author: Rob Walling
source.work: The Stair Step Method of Bootstrapping

heuristic: Make your first product a simple add-on to an existing ecosystem (a WordPress plugin, Shopify app, or Heroku add-on) with built-in discovery through its marketplace, marketed through a single traffic channel, instead of a stand-alone SaaS you must both build and market alone.

source.author: Rob Walling
source.work: The Stair Step Method of Bootstrapping

heuristic: You are probably undercharging: price on the value delivered and keep raising prices, because your best customers will be happier for it.

source.author: Patrick McKenzie (with Ramit Sethi)
source.work: Why Your Customers Would Be Happier If You Charged More

heuristic: Missing the billion-dollar outcome is not failure: define success as a sustainable business you actually want to run.

source.author: Sahil Lavingia
source.work: Reflecting on My Failure to Build a Billion-Dollar Company

heuristic: Ship many small projects quickly, let the market pick the winners, and double down only on the ones that get traction.

Give each launched MVP about one month to show signs of demand, and if it shows none, count it as failed and move to the next project; delivering a new product is the easy part, growing it fast is the hard part.
Commit only what you can afford to lose at each step, instead of sizing bets by projected returns.

source.author: Saras Sarasvathy

heuristic: Start from your means, who you are, what you know, and whom you know, rather than from an ideal market picked by analysis.

source.author: Saras Sarasvathy
source.note: SSRN bot-walls automated fetches (HTTP 403 challenge page). Reachable statement of the same principles: https://effectuation.org/the-five-principles-of-effectuation

heuristic: Competition is for losers: escape it by starting with a small market you can monopolize, then expand concentrically.
A bold, definite plan beats iterative tinkering: iteration without a committed view of the future will not take you from zero to one.
Market matters most: in a great market the market pulls product out of the startup, so get to product/market fit and do whatever is required to take it.

source.author: Marc Andreessen
source.work: The Pmarca Guide to Startups, part 4: The only thing that matters

heuristic: Cross the chasm by targeting a single beachhead niche and dominating it completely before expanding to adjacent segments.

source.author: Geoffrey A. Moore
source.note: The publisher page bot-walls automated fetches (HTTP 403). Reachable overview of the book and its beachhead strategy: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossing_the_Chasm

heuristic: Listening closely to your best customers can sink you: disruptive technologies start out worse on the metrics those customers value and win anyway.

source.author: Joseph L. Bower and Clayton M. Christensen

heuristic: Investors fund trajectories, not snapshots: build investor relationships long before you raise so they can judge the line, not a single dot.

source.author: Mark Suster
source.note: Medium-hosted; the host bot-walls automated fetches (HTTP 403 via Cloudflare, verified with browser and crawler user agents). No Wayback snapshot was available at verification time (archive.org temporarily offline). Title and author are widely cited; the URL is the canonical publication.

heuristic: Pick the three attributes that make your product great, get those very right, and ignore everything else at launch.

source.author: Paul Buchheit
source.work: If your product is Great, it doesn't need to be Good

heuristic: Measure product/market fit with the share of users who would be very disappointed without your product, and hold off on scaling until you clear the 40% bar.

source.author: Rahul Vohra
source.work: How Superhuman Built an Engine to Find Product/Market Fit (First Round Review)

heuristic: After product-market fit, spend a third to a half of your time hiring; it is the highest-leverage founder work, and one mediocre hire can unwind a great team.
While blitzscaling, hire Ms. Right Now, not Ms. Right: recruit the manager who fits the current phase of growth instead of waiting for the perfect long-term hire.
Hire less and hire later: when work burdens you, try doing it yourself first and look for another way before adding people.

source.author: Jason Fried, David Heinemeier Hansson, and Matt Linderman
source.work: Getting Real: Hire Less and Hire Later

heuristic: Poor sales, not bad product, is the most common cause of failure: get one distribution channel to work and you have a great business; get none and the product does not matter.
Give the basic service away free to acquire customers efficiently through word of mouth, then charge the heaviest users for a premium version.

Remain stand-alone if you are very early in a very large market and have a good chance of being number one, because no acquirer can afford what you are worth; failing either test, selling is rational.
Decide up front whether you are in it for rich or for king and act consistently; when a life-changing offer arrives, taking the money can be the right call regardless of the market left on the table.

source.author: Jason Cohen
source.work: Rich vs. King in the Real World: Why I Sold My Company

heuristic: Run in founder mode: the conventional advice to hire good people and give them room to do their jobs damages founder-led companies; stay engaged beyond your direct reports.
Give away your Legos: scaling means handing pieces of your job to new people and finding a new one, and the anxiety that provokes is a sign the company is growing correctly.

source.author: Molly Graham
source.work: Give Away Your Legos and Other Commandments for Scaling Startups (First Round Review)

heuristic: The best time to sell is when you have many options and no need to sell; enter acquisition talks only when you are certain you want to sell and likely to get a price you will accept, not to see what price you can get.

source.author: Justin Kan
source.work: The Founder's Guide to Selling Your Company
source.note: The original justinkan.com post (November 2014) returns 404; this is the archived copy of the author's 2016 republication.

heuristic: In a big market with a short window, raising and spending heavily to win the market beats running lean; being frugal is a means, not the goal, and the only two priorities are winning the market and not running out of cash.

source.author: Ben Horowitz
source.work: The Case for the Fat Startup

heuristic: Err on the side of ideas where you will face competitors: a crowded market signals real demand and solutions that are not good enough, so enter it with a precise thesis about what the incumbents are overlooking; startups are exceptionally rarely killed by competitors.

Reaching product/market fit is easier in a pre-existing category where users already pull, searching, clicking, and spending, and where decent competitors already make a living; enter with a twist consumers fundamentally understand rather than creating a new category.
Do not rely on predictions or extensive planning: steer the venture with the resources you control and shape the future through actions taken with self-selected co-creators.

Spend as little money as possible and get big slow: the slower you burn through funding, the more time you have to learn, and a company still small in users and employees can still change its product.
Avoid distractions that pay: day jobs, consulting, and profitable side projects are the worst kind, because you will always interrupt the startup to answer the people paying you now.

When you set up the company, have every founder sign an agreement that everyone's ideas belong to the company and that the company is everyone's only job, and ask what IP agreements each founder signed before; an undiscovered prior claim can stall an acquisition and a financing at the same time.

Treat outside money as plan B: fund the startup with the cash on hand, a kept day job, and a smaller scope, because constraints drive innovation and investor expectations start to trump product quality.

source.author: Jason Fried, David Heinemeier Hansson, and Matt Linderman

heuristic: A company becomes the people it hires, not the plan it makes: stay obstinate about the vision, flexible about tactics, and judge people by how fast they evolve the plan rather than whether they execute it.

source.author: Vinod Khosla
source.work: Vinod Khosla on How to Build the Future

heuristic: It is much better to reject a good candidate than to accept a bad one: hold out for people who are smart and get things done, and if you cannot decide, the answer is no hire.

Fix the founder split at the start, equally or close to it: a company of great value takes 7 to 10 years to build, so variations in the first year do not justify materially different stakes, and four-year vesting with a one-year cliff, not an unequal split, is the protection if a founder leaves.

source.author: Michael Seibel
source.work: How to split equity among co-founders
source.note: The YC library page renders via JavaScript and serves no text to plain fetches; the essay text was read from a Wayback Machine snapshot of this URL.

heuristic: Keep the founder split dynamic through the bootstrapping stage: each participant's stake tracks the relative unpaid fair-market value of actual contributions and self-adjusts as people's input changes, and the model terminates into a fixed split once the company can pay everyone from revenue or a priced round.
